name: GeoToolbox KdBoxTree
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree (also GEOS 3.14.1 STR-tree, nanoflann 1.10.1, tidwall rtree.c)
workload: Static k-d tree supporting boxes: bulk-load plus range (box window) and nearest queries on point and box keys, 2D/3D, uniform/skewed/clustered/polygon/parcel and real shapefile datasets, 10^2 to 10^6 elements.
claimed_speedup: Quickest to bulk-load, fastest at range queries on box keys and (from 10^4 up) point keys, fastest at nearest queries on box keys; 'other indices need 1.5-4x more queries to pay for themselves, mostly because they build 2-4x slower'; at 10^6 about 1.5-2x ahead of nanoflann on point nearest. No per-library absolute times in README (raw TSV results are in a separate repo).
hardware: ASUS ROG Strix G16, Windows 11 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Static index only: bulk-load, no insert/erase. Stores an extra copy of spatial keys by default (StoreSpatialKeys); turning it off is about 1.2x slower at the largest sizes. Boost R*-tree is the most versatile (dynamic insert/erase, any dimension).
caveats: Benchmark author is also the author of KdBoxTree (first-party). Compilers named but flags and CPU model not stated. Results live in a separate GitHub Pages repo (ikolev21.github.io); README gives only prose rankings. Author patched GEOS to work around an MSVC slowdown. Project is a small personal repo.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ spatial index R-tree faster than Boost.Geometry benchmark github'

name: tidwall/rtree.c
workload: Dynamic R-tree insert/erase/reinsert then range queries on point and box keys (GeoToolbox suite, 2D/3D synthetic and real datasets).
claimed_speedup: Independent GeoToolbox comparison: 'faster than Boost at insert/erase/reinsert and at querying afterwards' (no ratio given); matches KdBoxTree at box range queries on moderate 2D datasets (~10^4-10^5). Own README: 151.3 ns/op insert, 242.4 ns/op search on 1M random points (no baseline).
hardware: ASUS ROG Strix G16, Windows 11 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Dimensions and scalar type fixed at compile time via macros; no bulk-load, so builds by insertion and is sensitive to input order; heaviest memory use of the indices tested; no nearest query in the comparison.
caveats: Win versus Boost is stated in prose only, no numbers on the page. Third-party suite but flags and CPU model not given. The project's own README benchmark has no baseline.

name: nanoflann
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree (point k-nearest and range queries)
workload: Point-key k-nearest and range queries over 2D/3D datasets, 10^2 to 10^6 points (GeoToolbox suite).
claimed_speedup: GeoToolbox: nanoflann is fastest at point nearest queries (KdBoxTree only overtakes at 10^6) and 'competitive at range queries on point keys' while Boost 'lags behind in query performance'; uses the least memory. Own README: ~50% faster queries than original FLANN.
hardware: ASUS ROG Strix G16, Windows 11 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Points only (boxes need a 2N-dimensional encoding costing ~2x); no erase; stores only indices into caller's dataset; no box nearest query.
caveats: Ratios against Boost are not quoted on the page. Benchmark by a competing index author, flags and CPU model missing. License SPDX per repo page said 'BSD'; BSD-2-Clause assumed from nanoflann's known license, verify.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ spatial index R-tree faster than Boost.Geometry' -> GeoToolbox README

name: trueform
baseline: CGAL (EPICK kernel; also libigl, MeshLib, VTK, nanoflann, Coal/FCL)
workload: Mesh geometry ops on 1M-triangle meshes: mesh-mesh intersection curves (2x1M), connected components, boundary paths, 50% decimation, boolean union vs MeshLib, k-NN vs nanoflann.
claimed_speedup: Mesh-mesh curves 7 ms, 233x vs CGAL EPICK; connected components 10x vs CGAL; boundary paths 11x vs CGAL; decimation 50x vs CGAL edge_collapse; boolean union 28 ms 6x vs MeshLib; self-intersection 37x vs libigl EPECK; k-NN 3x vs nanoflann.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 with Python/TS bindings; multithreaded (16 threads) versus presumably serial CGAL; exact predicates.
caveats: Vendor-run benchmark (Polydera); README table has the numbers, the full methodology page (trueform.polydera.com/cpp/benchmarks) was opened but gave no figures. Parallel vs serial comparison. Non-OSI noncommercial license (commercial license sold separately), so reference only. CGAL is not compared for Boost-style 2D spatial queries.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ polygon boolean operations faster than CGAL GEOS' -> polydera.com tutorial -> repo README

name: Manifold
baseline: CGAL Nef/PMP mesh booleans (and OpenSCAD's CGAL backend)
workload: Mesh boolean difference of spheres up to 1.31M triangles (axiolid cross-kernel benchmark); author's own test: sphere differences up to 8M triangles and Menger sponge vs OpenSCAD+CGAL.
claimed_speedup: Third-party axiolid benchmark, sphere-sphere 1.31M triangles: Manifold 2,816 ms vs CGAL 13,368 ms (about 4.7x, derived from page data). Author's blog (i7-3930K, GTX 1070, Ubuntu 20.04): single-thread 'an order of magnitude faster' than OpenSCAD fast-csg, GPU '100-1,000 times faster than the current OpenSCAD release'.
stars_or_usage: 2.2k stars; used by OpenSCAD and others
tradeoffs: Guarantees manifold output; TBB parallel (optionally CUDA); uses robust floating point rather than exact arithmetic.
caveats: Evidence is from a competitor's repo (axiolid, license not stated, which claims higher speed in other scenarios) with CPU/compiler unstated; Manifold's own README gives no numbers. Blog baseline is OpenSCAD (CGAL-based), not CGAL directly. Parallel versus serial CGAL. The MeshLib blog also reports Manifold beating CGAL.
found_via: WebSearch 'Manifold mesh boolean benchmark vs CGAL speedup elalish'

name: MeshLib
baseline: CGAL (also Manifold, libigl, MCut and 5 others)
workload: Mesh union of 2M-triangle Nefertiti models; dental scan of 280K triangles with defects.
claimed_speedup: Union ~0.093 s, about 3.5x faster than Manifold and 47x faster than CGAL; on dental scan 'CGAL hangs and MCut fails, while MeshLib finishes in 44 ms'.
tradeoffs: Multithreaded, CUDA for some ops; half-edge manifold-by-construction; bindings for C, C#, Python, WASM.
caveats: Vendor blog benchmark (company sells the product); compiler and flags not stated; raw data only in a downloadable PDF not opened. Source-available, free for non-commercial and educational use only (commercial licence required), so reference, not OSI. Default threading versus serial CGAL.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ polygon boolean operations faster than CGAL GEOS' -> meshlib.io blog

name: THST (Hierarchical spatial trees)
workload: Compile time of the benchmark program; also load/query time of 1M small boxes and 100K intersection queries (charts only).
claimed_speedup: 'benchmark compilation: 35,3 sec vs 1,4 sec' versus Boost. Load and query charts versus Boost.Geometry rtree exist as images only; page text reports 'competitive' results.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4870HQ 2.50GHz, 16 GB RAM, macOS Sierra
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++03; RTree plus 2D QuadTree; hierarchical queries, ray-box queries, custom allocators.
caveats: Speed claim is compile time; runtime numbers are only in PNG charts whose values could not be read. Compiler/flags not stated, benchmark setup copied from mloskot/spatial_index_benchmark. Old hardware and OS.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ spatial index R-tree faster than Boost.Geometry benchmark github'

name: TinyBVH
workload: SAH BVH build and single-ray primary/any-hit traversal on CPU; GPU traversal up to 5 billion rays/s on Sponza (RTX 5080 laptop).
claimed_speedup: README: 'builds a SAH BVH faster than Embree and Madmann91' and 'traces individual primary and any hit rays faster'; no numbers in text (chart image only).
tradeoffs: Header-only, no dependencies; AVX2/NEON wide BVH kernels; single-ray traversal only, a small part of Embree.
caveats: Author labels results 'preliminary'; no numeric values in README text. Baseline Embree is not in the category's baseline list and is not a Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS equivalent.
found_via: WebSearch 'github C++ header-only BVH OR kd-tree ... vs Embree OR CGAL AABB tree'
